strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies fundamental limitation of Group DRO when applied to CTC-based speech recognition, with compelling empirical evidence (Figure 1) of length distribution variance across languages

Principled technical contribution: Proposes two complementary, well-reasoned modifications (length-matched batching and smoothed maximization objective) with clear mathematical formulation showing Group DRO as limiting case

Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough evaluation across 5 language sets, 2 pre-trained models, and both balanced/unbalanced settings with consistent improvements (worst-language error reduction up to 65.9%, average error up to 47.7%)
Rigorous ablation study: Demonstrates necessity of both components with substantial performance degradation when either is removed (up to 151.9% increase in worst-language CER)
Insightful analysis: Figure 2 effectively illustrates how CTC-DRO prevents weight collapse that occurs in standard Group DRO, showing more stable and balanced weight distributions throughout training
Practical applicability: Minimal computational overhead with only scalar weight tracking; readily compatible with existing CTC-based training pipelines
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameter specifications, comprehensive appendices with language-specific results, and promise to release code and trained models
weaknesses: Limited component novelty: Length-matched batching is straightforward data engineering; smoothed objective uses standard constant-in-denominator smoothing technique without clear justification for the specific log(q_g + α)L_g functional form

Insufficient theoretical analysis: Lacks convergence guarantees, performance bounds, or principled explanation for why this particular smoothing form is optimal; Lagrangian analysis is mostly algebraic without deeper insights into when/why smoothing helps

Hyperparameter selection challenges: α chosen via grid search {0.1, 0.5, 1} without principled methodology; no sensitivity analysis or guidance for practitioners on new domains; batch duration parameter d also requires tuning

Limited evaluation scope: Only multilingual ASR evaluated despite claims of broader applicability to language modeling and video transcription; all experiments use same wav2vec 2.0 pre-training paradigm with CTC; missing comparisons with other fairness/robustness methods and simpler baselines

Concerning result patterns: One regression (XLS-R set 3); worst-performing language changes in 4 settings suggesting potential trade-offs rather than universal improvement; improvements often incremental (5-10% relative) in several settings

Inadequate design justification: Limited explanation for summing losses instead of averaging in length-matched batches; choice to multiply by |G| in line 21 of Algorithm 2 not principled; these design choices appear effective empirically but lack rigorous justification

Insufficient failure mode analysis: No characterization of when/why CTC-DRO struggles; missing analysis of which language properties predict method effectiveness; acknowledged that disparities are 'not eliminated' without deeper investigation

Evaluation metric limitations: Only CER and LID accuracy; no downstream task evaluation despite acknowledging that CER may not correlate with actual usefulness; no human evaluation or qualitative analysis of transcription quality changes

Experimental design issues: Language set selection based on baseline model performance percentiles introduces potential selection bias; hyperparameter tuning on development sets could overfit to these specific language combinations; no cross-dataset evaluation of generalization

Presentation complexity: Algorithm 2 is dense and difficult to parse; distinction between length normalization and smoothed objective could be emphasized earlier; missing error analysis of what types of mistakes change with CTC-DRO

strengths: Clearly identifies and articulates a concrete problem with applying group DRO to CTC-based multilingual ASR, with good illustration of motivating issues (e.g., audio length distributions across languages)

Demonstrates consistent empirical improvements across five language sets with two pre-trained models, achieving substantial worst-language CER reductions (up to 65.9%) and average CER improvements (up to 47.7%)
Proposes a practical algorithm with minimal computational overhead compared to group DRO, making it deployable in real-world scenarios
Includes ablation study showing both components (length-matched batching and smoothed objective) contribute meaningfully to final performance
Provides useful empirical analysis via Figure 2, showing CTC-DRO maintains more stable and evenly distributed group weights compared to group DRO's extreme oscillations
Generally well-written with clear presentation of motivation, background, and methodology
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Length-matched batching is a simple preprocessing strategy, and the smoothed maximization objective (Eq. 10) is a straightforward modification without principled justification for why log(q_g + α)L_g is the right functional form

Insufficient theoretical foundation: No convergence analysis, theoretical guarantees, or principled derivation of the smoothed objective; the Lagrangian analysis (Eq. 13-15) merely restates the proportionality q_g ∝ L_g - α without providing deep insights

Narrow experimental scope limited to multilingual ASR with only two baselines (standard training and group DRO); missing comparisons with other fairness/robustness methods mentioned in related work or simpler alternatives like direct per-token loss normalization

Lack of statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs reported; some improvements are modest (e.g., Set 3 MMS: 36.6→32.8), making statistical significance unclear

Questionable design choices insufficiently justified: Length-matched batching introduces hyperparameter d with no sensitivity analysis; multiplying losses by |G| lacks justification; smoothing parameter α requires tuning without principled selection method

Incomplete analysis of core claims: Paper argues CTC losses are incomparable due to sequence length but only shows length distributions differ; doesn't empirically validate that length-matched batching + summing actually reduces bias in loss estimation compared to direct per-token normalization

Ablation study reveals concerning behavior: Removing SMOOTH component causes catastrophic LID accuracy drops (13.2%-43.2%), suggesting potential implementation instability rather than a robustly designed algorithm

Failure cases inadequately addressed: Set 3 XLS-R shows average CER slightly worse with CTC-DRO (16.6% vs 16.4%), worst-performing language sometimes shifts between methods (Korean→Khmer), and group DRO's extreme failures in some settings lack explanation

Algorithm specification lacks clarity and reproducibility details: Conditions for weight updates (line 11) are confusing, batch sampling procedure is vague ('iteratively added until duration meets target'), and computational costs are not reported

Root cause not addressed directly: If CTC loss scales with sequence length, shouldn't the solution involve per-token or per-unit-length normalization rather than indirect fixes like summing losses in length-matched batches?

strengths: Clear and insightful problem diagnosis: identifies fundamental incompatibility between group DRO and CTC loss due to input-length scaling, with well-presented motivation (Figure 1)
Principled technical approach with theoretical grounding: smoothed maximization objective is a justified generalization of group DRO, supported by Lagrangian analysis and Hedge algorithm connection
Comprehensive experimental validation: 5 language sets, 2 pre-trained models, balanced/unbalanced data, 13/14 settings show average CER improvement with up to 65.9% worst-language error reduction
Thorough ablation study demonstrating necessity of both components, with substantial performance degradation when either is removed
Excellent visualization of mechanism (Figure 2): clearly shows CTC-DRO produces more stable and balanced group weights compared to group DRO's extreme oscillations
Practical utility with minimal computational overhead, making it readily adoptable by practitioners
Clear presentation and strong motivation throughout the paper
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components are incremental (length-matched batching is straightforward engineering; smoothed objective is modest modification of group DRO with log(qg+α) term choice lacking deep justification)
Incomplete treatment of smoothing parameter α: only 3 values tested without systematic sensitivity analysis, no guidance for practitioners in new domains, functional form choice underjustified

Limited evaluation scope: restricted to single benchmark (ML-SUPERB 2.0), only CTC models tested, claims of broader applicability to language modeling and video transcription are stated but completely unvalidated

Theoretical gaps: paper acknowledges irreducible loss component from linguistic/acoustic properties but doesn't directly address it; unclear why smoothing alone suffices without explicit irreducible loss handling

Insufficient analysis of edge cases: worst-performing language changes unexpectedly in 4 settings, Set 3 XLS-R shows slightly worse average CER (16.6% vs 16.4%), failure modes not thoroughly investigated
No statistical significance testing: missing error bars, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests; some improvements are modest and reliability is unclear
Hyperparameter tuning without validation: α and ηq tuned on development data without cross-validation; potential overfitting to these specific language sets with no sensitivity analysis provided

Underjustified design choices: why sum utterance-level losses rather than average? Ablation doesn't isolate length-matched batching from loss summation. Target batch duration precision effects unexplored

Limited baseline comparisons: only compares against group DRO and CTC baseline; no comparison with other robustness methods or with Gao et al. (2022) who explored DRO for ASR; no comparison with simpler alternatives
Secondary metric trade-offs: LID accuracy degrades in some cases (e.g., Set 2 MMS: 98.4%→98.2%); trade-offs between CER and LID not discussed

strengths: Clear problem formulation with well-motivated analysis of why group DRO fails on CTC-based multilingual ASR
Mathematically grounded smoothed maximization objective with proper Lagrangian derivation and connection to Hedge algorithm
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 language sets with both balanced and unbalanced data, scaling to 18 languages, and multi-seed robustness testing
Strong and consistent empirical results: worst-language CER improved across all settings (up to 47.1% relative reduction), average CER improved in 13/14 settings
Thorough ablation study clearly demonstrating necessity of both components (length-matching and smoothing)
Compelling analysis of model behavior showing stable group weights for CTC-DRO vs. concentration in group DRO (Figure 2)
Practical algorithm with minimal computational overhead (1.3%) and easy implementation requiring only scalar group weights
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameter specifications, dataset information, and promised code release
Careful treatment of confounding factors with analysis of best-language performance and no significant degradation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: length-matched batching is primarily engineering; smoothed objective is straightforward modification (adding α to denominator) rather than fundamental innovation
Narrow scope with evaluation only on multilingual ASR with CTC; claims of broader applicability (text classification, video transcription) lack any empirical validation
Theoretical gaps: no convergence analysis, no rigorous justification that length-matching sufficiently addresses CTC incomparability, interaction between length-matching and smoothing under-explained
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity with optimal α varying across datasets (0.1-1.0) and no principled guidance for practitioners; batch duration hyperparameter also sensitive (Table 14)
Missing empirical comparisons: dismisses alternative approaches (data rebalancing, weighted sampling, other robust methods) as unsuitable without experimental evidence
Noteworthy performance degradations not thoroughly discussed: average CER worsens in 1/14 settings (Set 3), LID accuracy drops significantly in some cases (Set 1 MMS: 97.4%→95.8%, Set 5: 96.3%→90.5%)
Limited statistical rigor: most main results single-seed, no confidence intervals, marginal improvements (1-2% in several cases) lack significance testing beyond one setting
Presentation issues: 27-page paper with key analyses relegated to appendix; could be more concise; Algorithm 1 timing/accumulation semantics could be clearer
Generalization concerns: requires pre-defined groups, only tested on subpopulation shift (not domain shift), unclear applicability to open-ended problems

Incomplete analysis of loss incomparability: Figure 1 shows distribution differences but doesn't deeply justify why length-matching sufficiently resolves incomparability; loss-based DRO approach not compared against group-relative metrics

strengths: Clear problem identification with rigorous analysis of Group DRO's limitations for CTC (Section 2.3, Equations 7-9, Figure 1)
Extensive experimental evaluation across 5 language sets + 18-language scaling with comprehensive ablations, multi-seed robustness analysis, and reproducibility details
Consistent improvements in worst-language error rates across all evaluated conditions (up to 47.1% relative improvement)
Insightful weight stability analysis (Figure 2) demonstrating superior group weight distributions compared to Group DRO
Practical efficiency with minimal computational overhead (~1.3% training time increase) and simple algorithm that's easy to implement
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: length-matched batching is stratified sampling; smoothing parameter α is a minor Hedge algorithm modification without principled justification for this specific form

Weak theoretical grounding for smoothing parameter: no explanation for why this particular smoothing scheme is optimal; α appears arbitrary (range 0.1-1.0 lacks principled selection strategy); different optimal values across datasets suggest lack of universality

Insufficient comparative analysis: alternatives (calibration, auxiliary models) dismissed without empirical evaluation; Appendix G tests only 4 variants on one dataset; no comparison with other recent robust optimization methods or loss calibration techniques
Overclaimed applicability: Section 8 claims broader applicability to text classification and video transcription without any empirical evidence; claims remain purely speculative

Concerning scaling behavior: Appendix H shows worst-case improvement drops from 47.1% (6 languages) to 8.9-9.2% (18 languages); average CER increases for MMS (+3.0%); suggests method effectiveness degrades with more groups, limiting practical utility

Experimental concerns: seed instability (Table 15: Set 3 XLS-R shows -1.5% mean improvement across 4 seeds); significant LID accuracy degradation in multiple cases (Set 5 MMS: 96.3%→90.5%); language set selection based on baseline CER percentiles introduces potential bias
Group definition dependency not addressed: requires pre-defined groups but provides no solutions for unknown/noisy group structures, misspecified assignments, or multiple groupings

Incomplete justification of length-matched batching mechanism: why total duration matching suffices is unclear; why this succeeds where per-utterance normalization fails (Appendix G) lacks principled explanation

Statistical rigor gaps: most results lack significance tests beyond single-seed evaluation; no confidence intervals despite observed variance; hyperparameter tuning burden not addressed despite claims of minimal costs
Presentation issues: 27-page paper obscures core contributions; main algorithm fits ~1 page; notation introduced informally (Lg); related work limited on recent multilingual ASR fairness literature

strengths: Clear problem identification: The paper precisely articulates why group DRO fails with CTC due to incomparable losses from input length scaling and linguistic/acoustic properties (Section 2.3, Figure 1)

Principled technical solution: The smoothed maximization objective has rigorous theoretical grounding (Equation 12) and proper connection to the Hedge algorithm, with clear analysis of desirable properties

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive experiments across 5 diverse language sets from ML-SUPERB 2.0 with both balanced and unbalanced settings, plus scaling to 18 languages; consistent improvements up to 47.1% worst-language CER reduction and 32.9% average improvement

Thorough ablation and analysis: Component ablations show necessity of both contributions; group weight visualization (Figure 2) clearly demonstrates the problem; robustness testing across multiple seeds; honest analysis of best-language performance to verify no significant degradation
Practical applicability: Minimal computational overhead (~1.3% increase), readily adoptable with existing pre-trained models, addresses real accessibility problem for underrepresented languages
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed algorithm descriptions, comprehensive hyperparameter documentation, dataset specifications, code/model release promised, wall-clock times reported
Well-executed presentation: Clear writing, effective figures and tables, logical argument flow, honest acknowledgment of limitations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Length-matched batching is straightforward engineering; smoothed objective amounts to adding regularization parameter α to group DRO; contribution is primarily in combination rather than individual components being novel

Incomplete fundamental solution: The paper acknowledges it cannot estimate irreducible loss components; length-matched batching is a workaround for length scaling; loss incomparability due to linguistic/acoustic properties only partially addressed

Scope limitations: Focused specifically on CTC-based multilingual ASR; broader applicability claimed but experimentally validated only in speech domain; CTC's length-scaling properties are somewhat domain-specific

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Smoothing parameter α requires dev set tuning; batch duration is another hyperparameter affecting results (see Table 14); adds tuning burden; sensitivity evident especially for XLS-R on larger language sets

Mixed empirical results: LID accuracy sometimes decreases; XLS-R on set 3 shows slightly higher average CER with CTC-DRO (17.7% vs 17.0%); average WER increases marginally for XLS-R on set 4; scaling to 18 languages shows smaller improvements than main experiments

Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares to group DRO and CTC baseline; no empirical comparison to other recent robust optimization methods for multilingual ASR; alternative approaches dismissed without experimental validation

Insufficient analysis of when method works best: Limited investigation of which language/dataset characteristics benefit most; no systematic analysis of marginal improvement cases; would help practitioners understand applicability

Group definition requirement: Requires pre-defined groups (acknowledged as future work); limits applicability when groups are unknown or incomplete; acknowledged but practically significant constraint
Statistical testing: Most results single-seed; multi-seed testing limited to 2 sets; formal significance tests only in Appendix F.5; more rigorous statistical validation would strengthen claims

Problem not fully solved: Paper acknowledges performance disparities not eliminated; improvements may be insufficient for practical deployment in many languages; frames honestly but limits impact claim
